action.description: One of 'publish', 'list', 'read', 'delete', 'open', 'pin', 'unpin', 'quickstart'. Omitting it means 'publish'. **Calls** in the description says what each one does and takes, except as noted here.

file_path.description: publish: the local page Claude publishes (.html, or .md only when a skill says so). For an Artifact created from an Artifact type, it is one of that Artifact's data files. With `asset: true`, it is the local file Claude uploads. A short, distinctive basename also serves as the title when nothing else gives one.

asset.description: publish with `url`: true uploads `file_path` (or each of `file_paths`) to that artifact's asset store instead of publishing it as the page — or, with `from_url` and `asset_ids` in place of `file_path`, copies those assets of another artifact into it server side (see **Calls**).

file_paths.description: publish with `asset: true` only: several local image, video, PDF, font, stylesheet or script files in place of `file_path`, up to 25 in one call, all into the artifact that `url` names; one approval covers the call, and the result lists each file's id and url, or why it was not uploaded. A CSV, Markdown, JSON or plain-text file, a symbolic or hard link, and a file outside the working directory each go in a call of their own with `file_path`.

from_url.description: publish with `asset: true`, in place of `file_path`: the SOURCE artifact's claude.ai URL — one the person can open.

asset_ids.description: publish with `asset: true` and `from_url` only: 1–10 distinct asset ids from the source artifact (from a `scope: "assets"` listing of it, or an upload result).

favicon.description: Deprecated; Claude omits it and uses `icon`.

icon.description: One short generic word for the artifact's browser-tab icon, such as chart, calendar, recipe, code or map: a plain signifier, never a product or brand name. Claude includes it on every page's first publish and omits it on a redeploy so the artifact keeps its icon, passing a new one only when the person asks. Ignored on an Artifact created from an Artifact type.

files.description: Supporting files to publish alongside the page, as a map {"published/path": "source/path" | {from, contentType} | {artifact, path, ver?} | null}. The key is what the HTML references. The source is a path on disk, or {from, contentType} when the type cannot be inferred from the published extension. An {artifact, path} source copies that Artifact's published file on the server: an Artifact the person can open, with its type carried over, never an HTML or XML document, and at most 4 source Artifact versions per publish. null removes that path on an update, and files left out are kept. A plain list publishes each file at its own spelling. Sources must be under the working directory or Claude's scratchpad directory. `preflight.js` at the artifact root is reserved: it runs against open pages when Claude publishes updates, and it must be a JavaScript module of at most 8 KiB whose default export is a function, or the publish is refused.

path.description: Path relative to the working directory (or to `root`, which may be a folder in your scratchpad directory); the file is served at this same path next to the page.

contentType.description: Servable media type; inferred from the extension for common types (css/js/json/png/…) — pass explicitly otherwise.

from.description: Source file path — relative to `root` (default: the working directory), or absolute under the working directory or your scratchpad directory.

contentType.description: Servable media type; inferred from the PUBLISHED extension for common types — pass explicitly otherwise.

artifact.description: Another artifact's claude.ai URL: the file is copied from ITS published files, server side — nothing is downloaded. You must be able to open that artifact.

path.description: The file's published path inside that Artifact, as a listing of its files prints it (not "index.html").

ver.description: A version of that Artifact to copy from instead of its current one — only versions you are served (its history, if you can edit it); omit for the current version.

edits.description: publish: small changes Claude makes to the file at `file_path` in this same call, instead of editing the file with Edit and publishing after. Use it on a page (add `url` to update an artifact from another conversation) or on one data file of an artifact made from a type (its `url`, with that file as `file_path`). Not allowed with `type_url` or `files`. Each old_str is text copied exactly from the file as it now stands and must occur in it exactly once; new_str takes its place (empty deletes it). The edits apply in order, all or none: the file is published with them and then saved with them on disk, so it stays the source for later changes; on a miss nothing is changed or published, and the result says which edit failed and why.

old_str.description: Text copied exactly from the file; must occur once.

root.description: The base directory that relative `files` sources resolve against, like a bundler root. It never changes the published path of a `files` entry. It is relative to the working directory, or absolute within it or within Claude's scratchpad directory. It requires `files`, except on an Artifact made from a type, where a data `file_path` is served at its path relative to `root`, unless a `files` map entry states its served path. Claude sends it with every such publish, set to the folder that holds the Artifact's files at their served paths.

pin.description: publish only: true also pins the published artifact to the person's claude.ai sidebar once it is published. Claude passes it only when the person asked for that. A failed pin never fails the publish, and the result says so.

limit.description: list only: the maximum number of artifacts to return (default 25).

page_token.description: list only: the `next_page_token` a listing of the same scope gave, to list the artifacts after it.

scope.description: list: which listing to return. 'mine' is the default. The others are 'shared', 'all', 'types', 'files' (with `url`) and 'assets' (with `url`, continued with `after`). See **Calls**.

type_query.description: list with scope 'types' only: limits the listing to the types whose title or description match this text best, ignoring case; a type that matches less well is left out, so a narrowed listing is not the whole catalog. Claude omits it when choosing a type for a request, unless a listing made without it says more types exist than it shows.

type.description: list only: the name of a published Artifact type, as a 'types' listing shows it (case does not matter). The listing then shows the Artifacts made from that type instead of the person's gallery. Claude passes this or `type_url`, not both.

intent.description: quickstart only (required): what is being made — 'document' (writing people will keep editing or pass around as text, such as a memo, plan, spec, proposal or notes), 'slides' (a deck or one slide), 'design' (a visual design or prototype on a canvas), 'other' (a page to look at or use: an explainer, a diagram, anything interactive, a dashboard that shows data, a spreadsheet, anything else, or unsure).

design_systems.description: quickstart only: false when a design system's link is already in hand (it is then read with its own call) or one was declined. Omitted or true, the result lists the design systems (not for a document) and, for slides or a design, attaches the default one's README.

title.description: publish: the fallback title for an HTML page whose file has no <title>. It is a name, not a summary, and Claude keeps it the same across redeploys. On a `type_url` create, it is the new Artifact's name: what the person called it, or a short descriptive name. If it is left out, the Artifact is named after the type.

description.description: publish: one sentence for the subtitle on the gallery card.

label.description: A short name for this publish, at most 60 characters (e.g. "Draft to legal"). Optional. It is a few words, not a description.

overwrite_unread.description: publish with `files` or `root` to an existing artifact: published paths this call may replace or remove although you have not read or listed them in this session. Every other path the call touches must be one you read by its `path`, saw in a file listing, or published yourself, and must not have changed since — otherwise nothing is sent and the refusal names each path. Name a path here only when the user asked for it to be replaced without looking at what is there; it never excuses a path that changed after you read it.

url.description: An existing artifact's claude.ai link (claude.ai/artifact/{id} or claude.ai/code/artifact/{uuid}); a chat, project or session link is not one, and `action: "list"` lists the person's artifacts. On a publish, it is the artifact to update in place, one the person owns or was given edit access to (a read of it says "writer"). Before publishing to an artifact this conversation has neither read nor published, Claude reads it (`action: "read"`) and builds on what comes back; a publish sent without that read is refused. A refusal that hands Claude the live version counts as that read: Claude merges its changes into that version and publishes the result, and never resends the refused content unchanged. Claude omits `url` for a new artifact or to redeploy a file this conversation already published. For read, delete and the other calls that take a URL, it is the artifact to act on.

type_url.description: publish: the Artifact type to create this new, private Artifact from (a link from a 'types' listing). Claude omits `url`. Any `file_path`/`files` passed become the new Artifact's own files beside the type's fixed ones. read (no `url`): the type to describe. list: the type whose Artifacts to list, or Claude names the type with `type` instead.

auto_open.description: Only with `type_url` and no `file_path`: when the new Artifact opens for the person. Claude passes "after_first_write" when it will fill the Artifact right after creating it with a files publish to its url, so the person does not first see it empty. The Artifact then opens on that first write. Otherwise Claude omits it, and the Artifact opens when created; Claude always omits it for a type whose content it writes through a connector, such as a Claude Docs document, since no publish or store write follows to open it.

prompt.description: read, for an artifact shared with the person: what Claude needs from it, which steers the isolated summary.

force.description: publish: a last-resort overwrite that **discards** the newer published version. On a conflict, Claude merges its changes onto the newer content that the rejection hands it and publishes again. Claude passes true only when the person explicitly said to discard that specific version, and the server may still refuse it over a version saved from inside the page.

out_dir.description: read with `path`: the directory to save into. The default is this artifact's folder in Claude's scratchpad directory, where saving needs no approval. A published file lands at <out_dir>/<published path>, and saving it outside that default folder asks the person first. An asset's file is named by its id plus its type's extension; saving it outside the default folder is an ordinary file save the person may be asked to approve.

path.description: read: the file's published path inside the artifact, exactly as a 'files' listing printed it ("index.html" is the page itself). The file is saved locally, the result says where, and a small text file's contents are included. It can instead be an uploaded asset's id (32 hex characters, from an 'assets' listing or an upload result), and that asset is saved to a local file. delete: the id of the one asset to remove.

paths.description: read: several published paths in place of `path`, up to 256 in one call. Each file is saved as a single `path` would be, and the result lists where each one landed, or why it could not be read, with small text files' contents included while they fit.

after.description: list with scope 'assets' only: the `next` value from a previous listing, passed to continue it.

page.description: read only: true returns the rendered page in cases where a read otherwise returns something else. A typed Artifact's read leaves out the type's own page.

capabilities.description: publish: the runtime capabilities this page declares, as {name: config}. Claude loads the `artifact-capabilities` skill before passing it. On a redeploy Claude omits the field to keep what the page has, and {} clears it.

contract.description: publish: the artifact's runtime version. Leaving it out keeps the current version (the default), 'latest' upgrades, and an exact version pins or rolls back. It changes how the published page behaves, so Claude passes it only when the author explicitly intends that change.

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

- `cd` carries to the next call only in the main session, if the command succeeds and ends inside the working directories. Outside them the shell returns to the start folder; otherwise it stays where it was. Prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- IMPORTANT: Avoid using this tool to run `cat`, `head`, `tail`, `sed`, `awk`, or `echo` commands, unless explicitly instructed or after you have verified that a dedicated tool cannot accomplish your task. Instead, use the appropriate dedicated tool as this will provide a much better experience for the user.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000 for a foreground command.
- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits. No `&` needed. You will be notified when it exits — do not poll its output file while waiting. Foreground `sleep` is blocked; use Monitor with an until-loop to wait on a condition.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- GitHub notifies the owner of any `@name` written in a PR, issue, or comment. Write a bare `@name` only for a real login you mean to notify. Put roles, placeholders, and code (`@human`, `@reviewer`, `@types/node`) in backticks or drop the `@`, even when copied from project files.
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- Do not commit files that likely contain secrets (.env, credentials.json, .claude/settings.local.json, etc). Warn the user if they specifically request to commit those files.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

run_in_background.description: Set to true to run this command in the background.

dangerouslyDisableSandbox.description: Set this to true to dangerously override sandbox mode and run commands without sandboxing.

tools.name: Edit
tools.description:
Performs exact string replacement in a file.

- You must Read the file in this conversation before editing, or the call will fail.
- `old_string` must match the file exactly, including indentation, and be unique — the edit fails otherwise. Strip the Read line prefix (line number + tab) before matching.
- `replace_all: true` replaces every occurrence instead.

new_string.description: The text to replace it with (must be different from old_string)

replace_all.description: Replace all occurrences of old_string (default false)

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

Only use this when you genuinely need all of it or the user asked for the whole file; otherwise read it in parts with offset and limit, or search it.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a listing from the system with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in a message from the system. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

1090	first posting on the profile's `account`, and its payee (after the rules), letter for letter; a transaction in
1091	`existing` with no posting on that account is ignored. The n-th row of the file with a given key is a duplicate when `existing` holds at least
1092	n transactions with that key, and new otherwise. So importing a file against what it produced before makes all
1093	its rows duplicates, two identical coffees on one day both import the first time, and if one of them is already
1094	in the book exactly one of the two is new. A row that fails never takes part. Duplicates are only reported, never
1095	in `transactions`.
1096	
1097	Putting the new transactions into the book is a separate step; the import itself does not look at the book, nor at
1098	whether the accounts exist.
1099	
1100	## Budgets
1101	
1102	I want to say "no more than 400 a month on food" and then ask, for any stretch of time, how I am doing. That is
1103	the `tallybook.budgets` module; the commands and the web interface come later, on top of it.
1104	
1105	```python
1106	from datetime import date
1107	from tallybook.budgets import Budget, BudgetError, BudgetLine, budget_status
1108	from tallybook.money import Money
1109	
1110	food = Budget("Expenses:Food", "month", Money.parse("400.00 USD"), date(2024, 1, 1))
1111	for line in budget_status([food], ledger, Period.parse("2024-03")):
1112	    print(line.pattern, line.actual, line.remaining, line.percent, line.over)
1113	```
1114	
1115	### A budget
1116	
1117	`Budget(pattern, period_kind, amount, start)` is an immutable value (hashable, equal when its four fields are).
1118	
1119	- `pattern` is text that selects accounts, see below.
1120	- `period_kind` is exactly `"month"`, `"quarter"` or `"year"`: calendar months, quarters (January to March, April
1121	  to June, July to September, October to December) and years.
1122	- `amount` is a `Money`: how much I may spend in each such period. It must be greater than zero.
1123	- `start` is a `datetime.date`. The budget is in force from the calendar period that contains `start`, whole
1124	  (a `start` of 2024-03-20 on a monthly budget means March 2024 is the first month, with its full allowance).
1125	  Periods before that one have no budget at all.
1126	
1127	Building a `Budget` with a bad pattern (text or not), a `period_kind` that is not one of the three words, an amount
1128	that is not a `Money` or is zero or negative, or a `start` that is not a `date` raises `BudgetError`, a
1129	`tallybook.errors.ValidationError` (code `validation`) whose message says what was wrong.
1130	
1131	### Which accounts a budget watches
1132	
1133	A pattern is an account path in which any segment may be `*`, meaning "any one segment". Every other segment is an
1134	ordinary account name segment (an upper-case letter, then letters, digits, `_` or `-`), separated by `:`. Nothing
1135	else is allowed: an empty pattern, an empty segment, a lower-case segment, `**` or `Expenses:Fo*` is a
1136	`BudgetError`. (Budget patterns are not the account patterns of queries or the chart: no `**`.)
1137	
1138	An account matches a pattern when the pattern's segments match the first segments of the account's path: the
1139	account is what the pattern names, or lies anywhere below it. So `Expenses:Food` matches `Expenses:Food` and
1140	`Expenses:Food:Dining:Cafe` but not `Expenses:Foods` and not `Expenses`; `Expenses` matches every expense
1141	account; `Expenses:*:Dining` matches `Expenses:Food:Dining`, `Expenses:Fun:Dining` and anything below them;
1142	`Expenses:*` matches `Expenses:Food` but not `Expenses` alone.
1143	
1144	Only expense accounts (root segment `Expenses`) are ever counted. A pattern that can only match other kinds of
1145	account, such as `Income`, is allowed and simply never has any spending.
1146	
1147	Only postings in the budget's own currency count. A posting in another currency to a matching account is
1148	ignored (nothing is converted, even when the ledger knows exchange rates).
1149	
1150	### The status of budgets
1151	
1152	`budget_status(budgets, ledger, period)` takes a list of `Budget`, a `tallybook.ledger.Ledger` and a
1153	`tallybook.dates.Period`, and returns a list of `BudgetLine`. The ledger is not changed.
1154	
1155	The spending of a budget in the period is the sum of the amounts of all postings dated within the period (both
1156	ends included) that go to a matching expense account in the budget's currency. An expense is positive, so a
1157	refund (a negative posting) lowers the spending and the total can even be negative. The spending is also kept per
1158	account.
1159	
1160	**Allowance in the period.** The period I ask about need not be the budget's own kind of period, or a whole
1161	number of them. Take every calendar period of the budget's kind (the one containing `start` and later ones) that
1162	overlaps the asked period; each counts for `overlapping days / days in that calendar period`; add those fractions
1163	and multiply the budget amount by the sum; round once, to a whole minor unit, to the nearest with an exact half
1164	going away from zero (half a cent becomes a cent). Examples, all with a start on or before the period:
1165	
1166	| budget | asked period | allowance |
1167	|---|---|---|
1168	| 300.00 USD month | `2024-03` | 300.00 USD |
1169	| 300.00 USD month | `2024-03-01..2024-03-15` | 145.16 USD (15 of 31 days) |
1170	| 100.00 USD month | `2024-Q1` | 300.00 USD |
1171	| 100.00 USD month | `2024-01-15..2024-02-14` | 103.11 USD (17/31 + 14/29 of a month) |
1172	| 900.00 USD quarter | `2024-02` | 286.81 USD (29 of the 91 days of Q1 2024) |
1173	| 1200.00 USD year | `2024-Q1` | 298.36 USD (91 of 366 days) |
1174	| 1200 JPY year | `2024-03` | 102 JPY (101.64 rounded) |
1175	
1176	A budget whose first calendar period starts after the asked period ends is not in force and gets no line at all
1177	in the result. One that starts inside the asked period counts only from its first calendar period on (a yearly
1178	budget of 1200.00 USD that starts 2024-01-01, asked about `2023-12-01..2024-01-31`, gives 31/366 of the year:
1179	101.64 USD).
1180	
1181	**The lines.** A `BudgetLine` is an immutable value with these attributes:
1182	
1183	| attribute | meaning |
1184	|---|---|
1185	| `pattern`, `period_kind` | copied from the budget |
1186	| `budget` | the `Money` allowance for the asked period, as above |
1187	| `actual` | `Money`, the spending, in the budget's currency (zero when there is none) |
1188	| `remaining` | `Money`, `budget - actual` (negative when overspent) |
1189	| `percent` | a `decimal.Decimal` with exactly one decimal place: `actual / budget * 100` |
1190	| `over` | `True` when `actual` is strictly greater than `budget`, else `False` |
1191	| `accounts` | a tuple of `(account_path, Money)` pairs, one for each matching expense account whose spending in the period is not zero, sorted by path as plain text |
1192	
1193	`percent` is rounded to the nearest tenth with an exact half going away from zero (0.25 becomes `0.3`, -0.25
1194	becomes `-0.3`; a result of zero is `0.0`, never `-0.0`). For example, 0.01 USD against a 4.00 USD allowance is
1195	0.25 percent and shows `0.3`; 0.05 USD is 1.25 percent, `1.3`; 0.03 USD is 0.75 percent, `0.8`; 340.00 against
1196	400.00 is `85.0`, 450.00 is `112.5`, nothing spent is `0.0`, a refund-only period gives a negative percent such as
1197	`-2.5`. If the allowance itself came out as zero (a tiny budget asked about a short period), `percent` is `0.0`
1198	when nothing was spent and `100.0` otherwise.
1199	
1200	`BudgetLine.to_dict()` gives the JSON-able form, with these keys: `pattern`, `period_kind`, `budget`,
1201	`actual`, `remaining` (each money as `{"amount": "340.00", "currency": "USD"}`), `percent` (text, such as
1202	`"85.0"`), `over` (a boolean) and `accounts` (a list of `{"account": ..., "amount": {money}}` in the same order
1203	as the tuple).
1204	
1205	**Order.** The lines come sorted by `pattern` (plain text order), then by period kind in the order month,
1206	quarter, year, then by `start`. Budgets equal on all three keep the order I gave them in.
1207	
1208	**Several budgets.** Each budget gets its own line and counts independently: if two budgets match the same account
1209	(say `Expenses` and `Expenses:Food`) the same spending is in both lines, and two exactly alike budgets give two
1210	identical lines.
1211	
1212	### Examples worth checking
1213	
1214	With a ledger holding, in March 2024, 250.00 USD of spending on `Expenses:Food:Groceries`, 90.00 USD on
1215	`Expenses:Food:Dining` and a refund of 10.00 USD on `Expenses:Food:Groceries`, the budget above (400.00 USD a
1216	month from 2024-01-01) over `2024-03` gives `actual` 330.00 USD, `remaining` 70.00 USD, `percent` `82.5`, `over`
1217	False and `accounts` equal to `(("Expenses:Food:Dining", 90.00 USD), ("Expenses:Food:Groceries", 240.00 USD))`. A 300.00 USD budget gives `remaining` -30.00 USD, `percent` `110.0`, `over` True; one exactly used up is not over (`100.0`).
1218	
1219	## Recurring transactions
1220	
1221	Rent, the phone bill, the yearly insurance, a standing order to the savings account: they happen on a rhythm and
1222	I am tired of typing them in. In `tallybook.recurring` I want to write the rhythm in plain words, attach a
1223	transaction as a template, and get dated copies of it for any stretch of time I ask about. This module only works
1224	out the dates and the copies; storing them (and never making a copy twice) is the storage layer's job.
1225	
1226	```python
1227	from datetime import date
1228	from tallybook.recurring import Recurring, parse_schedule, occurrences, expand
1229	
1230	rent = Recurring("rent", "monthly on 1", template, start=date(2024, 1, 1))
1231	occurrences(rent, date(2024, 3, 1), date(2024, 5, 31))    # [2024-03-01, 2024-04-01, 2024-05-01]
1232	expand([rent, phone], date(2024, 3, 1), date(2024, 3, 31))  # dated Transactions
1233	```
1234	
1235	All dates are `datetime.date`; nothing here looks at the clock.
1236	
1237	### The schedule words
1238	
1239	`parse_schedule(text)` returns a `Schedule` and understands exactly these shapes:
1240	
1241	| text | meaning |
1242	|---|---|
1243	| `daily` | every day |
1244	| `weekly on mon` | every Monday; the day is `mon tue wed thu fri sat sun` |
1245	| `monthly on 5` | the 5th of every month; a number from 1 to 31 |
1246	| `monthly on last` | the last day of every month |
1247	| `yearly on 03-15` | every 15 March; `MM-DD`, two digits each |
1248	| `every 2 weeks from 2024-01-03` | the given date, then every 2 weeks after it |
1249	| `every 3 months from 2024-01-31` | the given date, then every 3 months after it |
1250	
1251	The `every` form is `every N UNIT from DATE`: `N` is a whole number of at least 1, `UNIT` is `days`, `weeks`,
1252	`months` or `years` (or the singular `day`, `week`, `month`, `year`, with any `N`), and `DATE` is a real
1253	`YYYY-MM-DD` date.
1254	
1255	Capitals and the amount of blank space between the words or around the text do not matter (`Monthly On LAST` is
1256	fine). Anything that is not one of these shapes (`daily on mon`, `weekly`, `monthly on 0`, `monthly on 32`,
1257	`weekly on someday`, `yearly on 13-01`, `yearly on 02-30`, `yearly on 3-15`, `every 0 days from 2024-01-01`,
1258	`every 2 weeks`, `every 2 fortnights from 2024-01-01`, `every 2 weeks from 2024-02-30`, an empty text, a value
1259	that is not text) raises `RecurringError`, a `tallybook.errors.ValidationError` (code `validation`), whose message
1260	names the shapes that are allowed.
1261	
1262	A `Schedule` is an immutable, hashable value; schedules that mean the same are equal (`Daily` and `daily`, or
1263	`every 1 week from 2024-01-03` and `every 1 weeks from 2024-01-03`). `str(schedule)` is the canonical text: lower
1264	case, single spaces, `monthly on last`, `yearly on 03-15` with two digits, and in the `every` form the unit
1265	singular when `N` is 1 and plural otherwise (`every 1 week from 2024-01-03`, `every 2 weeks from 2024-01-03`).
1266	Parsing the canonical text gives back an equal schedule.
1267	
1268	`schedule.between(start, end)` is the list of the schedule's own dates from `start` to `end`, both included,
1269	ascending (a Schedule knows nothing about a series' start, end or count).
1270	
1271	### Which dates a schedule produces
1272	
1273	- `daily`: every day. `weekly on mon`: every date that is a Monday.
1274	- `monthly on N`: the Nth day of every month; a month too short for it gets its last day, so `monthly on 31` gives
1275	  31 Jan, 29 Feb 2024, 31 Mar, 30 Apr and `monthly on 30` gives 28 Feb 2023. `monthly on last` is the last day
1276	  whatever the length.
1277	- `yearly on MM-DD`: that day every year; `yearly on 02-29` gives 29 Feb in leap years and 28 Feb in the others.
1278	- `every N days from D` and `every N weeks from D` (a week is 7 days): D, D plus N days (or weeks), plus twice
1279	  that, and so on; nothing before D. `every 10 days from 2024-01-01` gives 1, 11, 21, 31 January, 10 February.
1280	- `every N months from D` and `every N years from D` (a year is 12 months): the k-th date is D moved forward by
1281	  k times N months, counted from D itself and not from the previous date, the day clamped to the end of the month
1282	  when needed; nothing before D. So `every 1 months from 2024-01-31` gives 01-31, 02-29, 03-31, 04-30, 05-31 (no
1283	  drift to the 30th), `every 3 months from 2024-01-31` gives 2024-01-31, 04-30, 07-31, 10-31, 2025-01-31, and
1284	  `every 1 years from 2024-02-29` gives 2024-02-29, then 28 Feb 2025, 2026 and 2027, then 2028-02-29.
1285	
1286	### A recurring item
1287	
1288	`Recurring(name, schedule, template, start, end=None, count=None)`:
1289	
1290	- `name`: text of ASCII letters, digits, `-` and `_`, not beginning with `-` or `_` (`rent`, `phone-bill`, `2024_tax`).
1291	- `schedule`: a `Schedule`, or text, which is parsed with `parse_schedule` (so a bad text raises
1292	  `RecurringError`). The attribute `.schedule` is always a `Schedule`.
1293	- `template`: a `tallybook.model.Transaction`. Its own date means nothing; its payee, narration, flag, tags and
1294	  postings are what the copies are made from.
1295	- `start`: the first day the series may produce a date. `end`: the last day, included, or `None`. `count`: the
1296	  most dates the series ever produces, or `None`; it counts the dates produced from `start` on, so it never
1297	  depends on which stretch of time is asked about later.
1298	
1299	The attributes `.name .schedule .template .start .end .count` are readable. Items with equal attributes are equal.
1300	Anything wrong (a name that does not fit, a schedule that is not a `Schedule` or text, a template that is not a
1301	`Transaction`, a `start` that is not a date, an `end` that is not a date or is before `start`, a `count` that is
1302	not an `int` of at least 1, `True` included) is a `RecurringError`.
1303	
1304	`occurrences(rec, start, end)` returns the dates of the series within the window `start` to `end`, both
1305	included, ascending, as a list (an `end` before `start` gives `[]`). The series is the schedule's dates that are
1306	on or after `rec.start`, up to and including `rec.end` if there is one, and no more than `rec.count` of them,
1307	counted from the first. Some consequences:
1308	
1309	- A start on a day the schedule hits includes that day (`weekly on mon` from Monday 2024-01-01 gives 2024-01-01
1310	  first); `monthly on 5` starting 2024-02-10 gives 2024-03-05 first.
1311	- With `count=3`, a January start and `monthly on 5`, the dates are 5 Jan, 5 Feb, 5 Mar, even when I ask only
1312	  about April to June (nothing comes back then).
1313	- `end` and `count` both apply; whichever stops the series first wins.
1314	- The `every` forms keep the rhythm of the date after `from` even if the item starts later: `every 2 weeks from
1315	  2024-01-03` with `start=2024-01-20` gives 2024-01-31, 2024-02-14, 2024-02-28... (and never anything before
1316	  2024-01-03, even when `start` is earlier).
1317	
1318	### Copies of the template
1319	
1320	`expand(recs, start, end)` returns a list of new `Transaction` objects, one for every date of every item in the
1321	window, ordered by date, then item name (plain text order), then the item's position in `recs`. A copy has:
1322	
1323	- `date` the occurrence date; `payee`, `narration` and `flag` equal to the template's; `id` `None`;
1324	- `postings`: a new list holding the template's postings in order (a posting without an amount stays without one);
1325	- `tags`: a tuple of the template's tags plus the tag `recurring`, each once, sorted.
1326	
1327	The template is never changed, and changing a copy's list of postings changes neither the template nor the other
1328	copies. `instantiate(rec, on)` builds the single copy dated `on` the same way (it does not check that `on` is one
1329	of the item's dates).
1330	
1331	For example, with a template tagged `home`, `expand([rent], date(2024, 2, 1), date(2024, 3, 31))` for the item
1332	above gives two transactions dated 2024-02-01 and 2024-03-01, each with tags `("home", "recurring")`.
1333	
1334	### Two more helpers
1335	
1336	`next_occurrence(rec, after)` returns the first date of the series (`start`, `end` and `count` applied as for
1337	`occurrences`) strictly after the date `after`, or `None` when the series has no more dates. For `monthly on 5`
1338	starting 2024-01-01, `after` 2024-02-05 gives 2024-03-05 and `after` 2023-06-01 gives 2024-01-05.
1339	
1340	`describe(schedule)` says a schedule in words for a person:
1341	
1342	| schedule | text |
1343	|---|---|
1344	| `daily` | `every day` |
1345	| `weekly on mon` | `every Monday` (`Tuesday`, `Wednesday`, `Thursday`, `Friday`, `Saturday`, `Sunday`) |
1346	| `monthly on 5` | `on the 5th of every month` |
1347	| `monthly on last` | `on the last day of every month` |
1348	| `yearly on 03-15` | `every year on 15 March` |
1349	| `every 2 weeks from 2024-01-03` | `every 2 weeks from 2024-01-03` |
1350	| `every 1 month from 2024-01-31` | `every month from 2024-01-31` |
1351	
1352	A day of the month is an English ordinal (1st, 2nd, 3rd, 4th, 11th, 12th, 13th, 21st, 22nd, 23rd, 31st); a day in
1353	`yearly on` is a plain number (`every year on 5 July`). In the `every` form a step of 1 drops the number and uses
1354	the singular unit (`every day from DATE`, `every week`, `every month`, `every year`); other steps keep the number
1355	and the plural unit (`every 3 months from ...`).
1356	
1357	## Reports
1358	
1359	This is what I really want the tool for: look at the book and tell me where I stand. In `tallybook.reports` I
1360	want six reports, each a plain Python `dict` I can `json.dumps` straight away, a function that draws any of them as
1361	text, and one that turns them into CSV.
1362	
1363	```python
1364	from tallybook.reports import (trial_balance, balance_sheet, income_statement, cashflow, register, net_worth,
1365	                               render_text, report_to_csv, ReportError)
1366	
1367	report = income_statement(ledger, Period.parse("2024-03"))
1368	print(render_text(report), end="")
1369	```
1370	
1371	Every report function takes a `tallybook.ledger.Ledger` first and does not change it. `ReportError` is a
1372	`tallybook.errors.ValidationError` (code `validation`).
1373	
1374	### Conventions all reports share
1375	
1376	- A report `dict` contains only dicts, lists, strings, booleans, `None` and integers. Its key `"report"` is
1377	  `"trial_balance"`, `"balance_sheet"`, `"income_statement"`, `"cashflow"`, `"register"` or `"net_worth"`.
1378	- Money is always `{"amount": "12.50", "currency": "USD"}` (amount text with the currency's own number of
1379	  decimals, a leading `-` when negative, no thousands separators). Dates are `"YYYY-MM-DD"` text.
1380	- The type of an account comes from its first path segment: `Assets` asset, `Liabilities` liability, `Equity`
1381	  equity, `Income` income, `Expenses` expense.
1382	- Lists of accounts are sorted by account path as plain text, character by character (`Expenses:Food-X` comes
1383	  before `Expenses:Food:Alpha` because `-` sorts before `:`), then by currency code; lists of money per currency by
1384	  currency code. Postings are never rolled up into parent accounts unless stated.
1385	- A zero balance is left out of an account list. (Lists of money per currency are described report by report.)
1386	- Dates mean whole days, both ends of a `Period` included. A "balance on D" counts every posting dated on or
1387	  before D.
1388	- Percentages are text with exactly one decimal (`"5.7"`, `"100.0"`, `"-2.5"`), rounded to the nearest tenth of a
1389	  percent, an exact half going away from zero (0.25 becomes `0.3`); a zero result is `"0.0"`, never `"-0.0"`.
1390	- Converting to one currency (`convert_to="EUR"`) uses the exchange rates the ledger knows: its attribute `rates`,
1391	  the `RateTable` it was created with (an empty table if none), at the rate in force on the date given below, one
1392	  amount at a time, as the currency module converts money. A missing rate raises the currency module's own
1393	  `CurrencyError` as it is, and so does a `convert_to` that is not a known currency.

1411	### trial_balance(ledger, as_of)
1412	
1413	`as_of` is a date, or `None` for every posting. The result:
1414	
1415	```
1416	{"report": "trial_balance", "as_of": "2024-03-31",
1417	 "accounts": [{"account": "Assets:Cash", "type": "asset", "debit": {money}, "credit": null}, ...],
1418	 "totals": [{"currency": "USD", "debit": {money}, "credit": {money}, "balanced": true}]}
1419	```
1420	
1421	`as_of` is `null` when `None` was given. `accounts` has one entry per account and currency whose balance is not
1422	zero: a positive balance is in `debit` (`credit` is `null`), a negative one as its absolute value in `credit`
1423	(`debit` is `null`). `totals` has one entry per currency appearing in `accounts`: the sum of the debits, the sum of
1424	the credits, and `balanced`, true when the two are equal. For the sample book on 2024-03-31 the single total is
1425	4400.00 and 4400.00. An empty ledger gives empty lists.
1426	
1427	### balance_sheet(ledger, as_of, convert_to=None, today=None)
1428	
1429	```
1430	{"report": "balance_sheet", "as_of": "2024-03-31", "currency": null,
1431	 "assets":      {"accounts": [{"account": "Assets:Cash", "balance": {money}}, ...], "total": [{money}, ...]},
1432	 "liabilities": {"accounts": [...], "total": [...]},
1433	 "equity":      {"accounts": [...], "retained_earnings": [{money}, ...], "total": [...]},
1434	 "balanced": true}
1435	```
1436	
1437	- `as_of` is a date or `None` (everything); `currency` is `convert_to` or `null`.
1438	- Assets, liabilities and equity each list the accounts of that type with a non-zero balance, one entry per
1439	  account and currency. An asset balance is the sum of its postings; a liability or equity balance has its sign
1440	  turned round, so money owed is positive.
1441	- `retained_earnings` is income less expenses of every posting up to `as_of`, per currency, as a list of money
1442	  sorted by currency without zero results. It is part of `equity.total`, which makes the sheet balance.
1443	- `total` of a section is a list with the sum of the section's lines for each currency that has a line (for
1444	  equity also the retained earnings), sorted by currency; `[]` when the section has nothing.
1445	- `balanced` is true when for every currency `assets.total` equals `liabilities.total` plus `equity.total`
1446	  (a missing currency counts as zero).
1447	- With `convert_to`: every account line is converted separately at the rate on `as_of` (a line already in
1448	  `convert_to` is left as it is) and becomes `{"account", "balance": converted money, "original": the money
1449	  before converting}`; each retained-earnings amount is converted separately and they are added into a single
1450	  entry (a list of one) when any was non-zero; every `total` is then a list of exactly one money in `convert_to`,
1451	  zero if the section is empty. `balanced` is computed on the converted figures. Converting needs a date:
1452	  `convert_to` with `as_of=None` is a `ReportError`.
1453	- `today` is accepted for the day the command line and the web interface will pass, and has no effect.
1454	
1455	### income_statement(ledger, period, convert_to=None)
1456	
1457	```
1458	{"report": "income_statement", "start": "2024-03-01", "end": "2024-03-31", "currency": null,
1459	 "income":   {"accounts": [{"account": "Income:Salary", "amount": {money}, "percent": "100.0"}], "total": [{money}]},
1460	 "expenses": {"accounts": [...same line shape...], "total": [{money}]},
1461	 "net": [{money}]}
1462	```
1463	
1464	Only postings dated within `period` to income or expense accounts count. An income amount has its sign turned
1465	round (earning 2500.00 is `2500.00`), an expense is as it is. Each section lists one line per account and
1466	currency with a non-zero amount; `percent` is the line's share of the section total in the same currency (`"0.0"`
1467	when that total is zero; a negative line, a refund, gives a negative percentage). `total` is the list of section
1468	sums per currency that have a line, `[]` when there is none. `net` has, for every currency in either total, income
1469	less expenses, sorted by currency (zero included).
1470	
1471	With `convert_to` each line is converted separately at the rate on the last day of the period and gets an
1472	`"original"` key holding the money before converting; the totals and `net` are then single-entry lists in
1473	`convert_to` (zero if empty), and the percentages are shares of the converted totals.
1474	
1475	### cashflow(ledger, period)
1476	
1477	Cash means all asset accounts together; what went in and out is told by the account on the other side of each
1478	transaction. For every transaction dated in the period, work per currency: sum its postings to asset accounts;
1479	when that sum is not zero, every posting of the same currency to a non-asset account moves the opposite of its own
1480	amount into the category that account names (a salary posting of -2500.00 puts +2500.00 in, an expense posting of
1481	+54.50 puts -54.50, a card payoff posting of +900.00 on `Liabilities:Card` puts -900.00). A transaction that only
1482	moves money between asset accounts (sum zero) contributes nothing. Then, per account and currency, the
1483	contributions of the period are added: a positive result is an inflow, a negative one an outflow (shown as a
1484	positive amount), zero is left out.
1485	
1486	```
1487	{"report": "cashflow", "start": "2024-03-01", "end": "2024-03-31",
1488	 "opening": [{money}], "inflows": [{"account": "Income:Salary", "amount": {money}}],
1489	 "outflows": [{"account": ..., "amount": {money}}], "total_in": [{money}], "total_out": [{money}],
1490	 "net": [{money}], "closing": [{money}]}
1491	```
1492	
1493	`opening` is the asset balance before the period starts, `closing` the one after its last day, `net` the change
1494	(`total_in - total_out`, equal to `closing - opening`). The money lists (`opening`, `total_in`, `total_out`, `net`,
1495	`closing`) have one entry for every currency of any asset posting dated on or before the end of the period (zero
1496	included), sorted by currency; `inflows` and `outflows` are sorted by account then currency. In the sample, March has
1497	opening 1000.00, inflow Salary 2500.00, outflow Food 54.50 (the transfer to Cash cancels, Cash spending counts),
1498	closing 3445.50; April has opening 3445.50, no inflow, outflows Food 30.00 and `Liabilities:Card` 900.00, closing
1499	2515.50.

1501	### register(ledger, account, period=None, rollup=False)
1502	
1503	The postings of one account, in order, with a running balance. `account` must exist in the ledger's chart (a
1504	parent such as `Assets` exists when a sub-account does), otherwise `ReportError`. Without `rollup` only postings to
1505	exactly that account are listed; with `rollup=True` also those to accounts below it.
1506	
1507	```
1508	{"report": "register", "account": "Assets:Bank:Checking", "rollup": false, "start": "2024-03-01", "end": "2024-03-31",
1509	 "opening": [{money}], "rows": [{"date": "2024-03-01", "id": 2, "payee": "Acme", "narration": "",
1510	   "account": "Assets:Bank:Checking", "amount": {money}, "balance": {money}}, ...], "closing": [{money}]}
1511	```
1512	
1513	`start` and `end` are the period's days, or `null` without a period (then every posting is listed). `rows` are
1514	ordered by date, then transaction id, then the posting's place in its transaction; with a period, only postings
1515	inside it. `balance` is the running balance of that row's currency over the selected accounts, from `opening`
1516	through this row. `opening` is the balance of the selection before `start` (zero when there is no period);
1517	`closing` is the balance after the last row of the period (nothing later counts). Both are lists with one money
1518	for every currency of any selected posting dated on or before `end`, zero included, sorted by currency.
1519	
1520	### net_worth(ledger, period, step="month")
1521	
1522	How my wealth moved over time. `step` is `"week"`, `"month"`, `"quarter"` or `"year"` (anything else is a
1523	`ReportError`). The steps are exactly those `tallybook.dates.periods(period.start, period.end, step)` gives (whole
1524	calendar steps touching `period`, the first and last not cut down to it); a point is made for the end of each.
1525	
1526	```
1527	{"report": "net_worth", "start": "2024-01-15", "end": "2024-04-10", "step": "month",
1528	 "points": [{"date": "2024-01-31", "assets": [{money}], "liabilities": [{money}], "net": [{money}]}, ...]}
1529	```
1530	
1531	`start` and `end` are the period's. Each point has `date`, the last day of the step, and three lists of money with
1532	one entry per currency of any asset or liability posting dated on or before that date (zero included), sorted by
1533	currency: `assets` the sum of the asset balances, `liabilities` the sum of the liability balances turned positive
1534	(money owed), `net` the first less the second. A date before any asset or liability posting gives empty lists.
1535	For the sample book and `2024-01-15..2024-04-10` the points are 2024-01-31 (assets 1000.00, liabilities 0.00, net
1536	1000.00), 2024-02-29 (the same), 2024-03-31 (3445.50, 900.00, 2545.50) and 2024-04-30 (2515.50, 0.00, 2515.50).

1540	`report_to_csv(report)` turns any report dict into CSV for a spreadsheet: the report's table part, written as

1542	column and an amount column of plain amount text; totals are not included; percent cells are the plain percent

1649	## Export, and the plain text tables
1650	
1651	I want to get my transactions out of the book in two formats other tools can read, and I want every text report
1652	(they come next) laid out by one table routine that I can also call myself. All of it is `tallybook.export`:
1653	
1654	```python
1655	from tallybook.export import transactions_to_csv, transactions_to_json, render_table
1656	
1657	open("march.csv", "w", encoding="utf-8", newline="").write(transactions_to_csv(txs))
1658	print(render_table(["Name", "Qty"], [["Apple", 3], ["Kiwi", 12]], "lr"), end="")
1659	```
1660	
1661	`txs` is any iterable of `tallybook.model.Transaction`. These functions only read them, do not sort (the order is
1662	the order I give), return text and never write files.
1663	
1664	### CSV
1665	
1666	`transactions_to_csv(txs)` returns one record per **posting**, so a transaction with three postings is three
1667	records. The first record is always the header, exactly:
1668	
1669	```
1670	id,date,flag,payee,narration,tags,account,amount,currency,note
1671	```
1672	
1673	Each following record has these ten fields, in this order:
1674	
1675	| field | content |
1676	|---|---|
1677	| `id` | the transaction's id as a decimal number, empty when it has none (`None`) |
1678	| `date` | `YYYY-MM-DD` |
1679	| `flag` | `*` or `!` |
1680	| `payee`, `narration` | as stored |
1681	| `tags` | the tags sorted as plain text and joined with `;` (no spaces); empty for none |
1682	| `account` | the posting's account path |
1683	| `amount` | the amount without the currency, with the currency's own number of decimals and a leading `-` when negative, no thousands separators (`4.50`, `-4.50`, `900` for yen) |
1684	| `currency` | the currency code |
1685	| `note` | the posting's note |
1686	
1687	The first six fields repeat on every record of a transaction. A posting without an amount gives empty `amount`
1688	and `currency`. A transaction with no postings gives one record with its first six fields and the last four
1689	empty. No transactions give only the header record.
1690	
1691	Quoting is minimal. A field is wrapped in double quotes if, and only if, it contains a comma, a double quote, a
1692	carriage return or a line feed; a double quote inside it is doubled. Spaces or tabs alone never cause quoting,
1693	and non-ASCII text is written as it is. Records end with a single `\n` (never `\r\n`), the last one too. So a book
1694	with a coffee in it gives
1695	
1696	```
1697	id,date,flag,payee,narration,tags,account,amount,currency,note
1698	7,2024-03-01,!,"Café, Bäcker","say ""hi""",a;lunch,Expenses:Food,4.50,USD,"a, b"
1699	7,2024-03-01,!,"Café, Bäcker","say ""hi""",a;lunch,Assets:Cash,-4.50,USD,
1700	```
1701	
1702	`to_csv(headers, rows)` is the same writer for any table of cells: header texts, then rows of cells; a cell is
1703	written with `str()` except `None`, which is an empty field. Same quoting and line endings, header first.
1704	
1705	### JSON
1706	
1707	`transactions_to_json(txs)` returns a JSON array with one object per transaction, in the given order:
1708	
1709	```
1710	{"id": 7, "date": "2024-03-01", "flag": "!", "payee": "Café, Bäcker", "narration": "say \"hi\"",
1711	 "tags": ["a", "lunch"],
1712	 "postings": [{"account": "Expenses:Food", "amount": {"amount": "4.50", "currency": "USD"}, "note": "a, b"}, ...]}
1713	```
1714	
1715	`id` is `null` when the transaction has none. `tags` is a list, sorted as plain text, each tag once. A posting's
1716	`amount` is the money object `{"amount": "4.50", "currency": "USD"}` (amount text as in the CSV), or `null` for a
1717	posting without one. Postings keep their order. The text is made like every JSON document in this project:
1718	`json.dumps(value, indent=2, sort_keys=True, ensure_ascii=False)` plus one `\n`; no transactions give `[]` and a
1719	newline.
1720	
1721	Three helpers make the same pieces available alone: `money_to_dict(money)` (the object above, `None` for
1722	`None`), `transaction_to_dict(tx)` (one transaction object as a dict) and `to_json(value)` (the text exactly as
1723	above, for any JSON-able value).
1724	
1725	### Tables
1726	
1727	`render_table(headers, rows, align=None)` returns fixed-width text.
1728	
1729	- `headers` and `rows` may be any iterables (list, tuple, generator); each row must have exactly as many cells
1730	  as there are headers. A cell is shown as `str(cell)`, except `None` which is empty. A tab, a carriage return or a
1731	  line feed inside a cell is shown as one space each, so a cell is always one line.
1732	- `align` is `None` (every column left aligned) or a string, list or tuple with one letter per column, `"l"` or
1733	  `"r"`: `"lrr"` or `["l", "r", "r"]`. A letter other than those two, or a length that is not the number of
1734	  columns, is an `ExportError`, and so is a row with the wrong number of cells. `tallybook.export.ExportError` is a
1735	  `tallybook.errors.ValidationError` (code `validation`).
1736	- A column is as wide as the longest of its title and its cells, a text's width being its `len()`.
1737	- The first line is the titles, the second a rule of `-` as wide as each column, then one line per row. Cells are
1738	  padded to the column width on the right when the column is left aligned and on the left when right aligned
1739	  (titles too), and joined with **two spaces**. Trailing spaces are then removed from every line. Every line, the
1740	  last included, ends with `\n`.
1741	- No rows give the titles and the rule only. No headers at all give the empty string (and then rows are not
1742	  looked at).
1743	
1744	For instance `render_table(["Name", "Qty", "Price"], [["Apple", 3, "1.50"], ["Kiwi", 12, "10.25"], ["Ünï", None, "x\ty"]], "lrr")`
1745	is
1746	
1747	```
1748	Name   Qty  Price
1749	-----  ---  -----

## Budgets

I want to say "no more than 400 a month on food" and then ask, for any stretch of time, how I am doing. That is
the `tallybook.budgets` module; the commands and the web interface come later, on top of it.

```python
from datetime import date
from tallybook.budgets import Budget, BudgetError, BudgetLine, budget_status
from tallybook.money import Money

food = Budget("Expenses:Food", "month", Money.parse("400.00 USD"), date(2024, 1, 1))
for line in budget_status([food], ledger, Period.parse("2024-03")):
    print(line.pattern, line.actual, line.remaining, line.percent, line.over)
```

### A budget

`Budget(pattern, period_kind, amount, start)` is an immutable value (hashable, equal when its four fields are).

- `pattern` is text that selects accounts, see below.
- `period_kind` is exactly `"month"`, `"quarter"` or `"year"`: calendar months, quarters (January to March, April
  to June, July to September, October to December) and years.
- `amount` is a `Money`: how much I may spend in each such period. It must be greater than zero.
- `start` is a `datetime.date`. The budget is in force from the calendar period that contains `start`, whole
  (a `start` of 2024-03-20 on a monthly budget means March 2024 is the first month, with its full allowance).
  Periods before that one have no budget at all.

Building a `Budget` with a bad pattern (text or not), a `period_kind` that is not one of the three words, an amount
that is not a `Money` or is zero or negative, or a `start` that is not a `date` raises `BudgetError`, a
`tallybook.errors.ValidationError` (code `validation`) whose message says what was wrong.

### Which accounts a budget watches

A pattern is an account path in which any segment may be `*`, meaning "any one segment". Every other segment is an
ordinary account name segment (an upper-case letter, then letters, digits, `_` or `-`), separated by `:`. Nothing
else is allowed: an empty pattern, an empty segment, a lower-case segment, `**` or `Expenses:Fo*` is a
`BudgetError`. (Budget patterns are not the account patterns of queries or the chart: no `**`.)

An account matches a pattern when the pattern's segments match the first segments of the account's path: the
account is what the pattern names, or lies anywhere below it. So `Expenses:Food` matches `Expenses:Food` and
`Expenses:Food:Dining:Cafe` but not `Expenses:Foods` and not `Expenses`; `Expenses` matches every expense
account; `Expenses:*:Dining` matches `Expenses:Food:Dining`, `Expenses:Fun:Dining` and anything below them;
`Expenses:*` matches `Expenses:Food` but not `Expenses` alone.

Only expense accounts (root segment `Expenses`) are ever counted. A pattern that can only match other kinds of
account, such as `Income`, is allowed and simply never has any spending.

Only postings in the budget's own currency count. A posting in another currency to a matching account is
ignored (nothing is converted, even when the ledger knows exchange rates).

### The status of budgets

`budget_status(budgets, ledger, period)` takes a list of `Budget`, a `tallybook.ledger.Ledger` and a
`tallybook.dates.Period`, and returns a list of `BudgetLine`. The ledger is not changed.

The spending of a budget in the period is the sum of the amounts of all postings dated within the period (both
ends included) that go to a matching expense account in the budget's currency. An expense is positive, so a
refund (a negative posting) lowers the spending and the total can even be negative. The spending is also kept per
account.

**Allowance in the period.** The period I ask about need not be the budget's own kind of period, or a whole
number of them. Take every calendar period of the budget's kind (the one containing `start` and later ones) that
overlaps the asked period; each counts for `overlapping days / days in that calendar period`; add those fractions
and multiply the budget amount by the sum; round once, to a whole minor unit, to the nearest with an exact half
going away from zero (half a cent becomes a cent). Examples, all with a start on or before the period:

| budget | asked period | allowance |
|---|---|---|
| 300.00 USD month | `2024-03` | 300.00 USD |
| 300.00 USD month | `2024-03-01..2024-03-15` | 145.16 USD (15 of 31 days) |
| 100.00 USD month | `2024-Q1` | 300.00 USD |
| 100.00 USD month | `2024-01-15..2024-02-14` | 103.11 USD (17/31 + 14/29 of a month) |
| 900.00 USD quarter | `2024-02` | 286.81 USD (29 of the 91 days of Q1 2024) |
| 1200.00 USD year | `2024-Q1` | 298.36 USD (91 of 366 days) |
| 1200 JPY year | `2024-03` | 102 JPY (101.64 rounded) |

A budget whose first calendar period starts after the asked period ends is not in force and gets no line at all
in the result. One that starts inside the asked period counts only from its first calendar period on (a yearly
budget of 1200.00 USD that starts 2024-01-01, asked about `2023-12-01..2024-01-31`, gives 31/366 of the year:
101.64 USD).

**The lines.** A `BudgetLine` is an immutable value with these attributes:

| attribute | meaning |
|---|---|
| `pattern`, `period_kind` | copied from the budget |
| `budget` | the `Money` allowance for the asked period, as above |
| `actual` | `Money`, the spending, in the budget's currency (zero when there is none) |
| `remaining` | `Money`, `budget - actual` (negative when overspent) |
| `percent` | a `decimal.Decimal` with exactly one decimal place: `actual / budget * 100` |
| `over` | `True` when `actual` is strictly greater than `budget`, else `False` |
| `accounts` | a tuple of `(account_path, Money)` pairs, one for each matching expense account whose spending in the period is not zero, sorted by path as plain text |

`percent` is rounded to the nearest tenth with an exact half going away from zero (0.25 becomes `0.3`, -0.25
becomes `-0.3`; a result of zero is `0.0`, never `-0.0`). For example, 0.01 USD against a 4.00 USD allowance is
0.25 percent and shows `0.3`; 0.05 USD is 1.25 percent, `1.3`; 0.03 USD is 0.75 percent, `0.8`; 340.00 against
400.00 is `85.0`, 450.00 is `112.5`, nothing spent is `0.0`, a refund-only period gives a negative percent such as
`-2.5`. If the allowance itself came out as zero (a tiny budget asked about a short period), `percent` is `0.0`
when nothing was spent and `100.0` otherwise.

`BudgetLine.to_dict()` gives the JSON-able form, with these keys: `pattern`, `period_kind`, `budget`,
`actual`, `remaining` (each money as `{"amount": "340.00", "currency": "USD"}`), `percent` (text, such as
`"85.0"`), `over` (a boolean) and `accounts` (a list of `{"account": ..., "amount": {money}}` in the same order
as the tuple).

**Order.** The lines come sorted by `pattern` (plain text order), then by period kind in the order month,
quarter, year, then by `start`. Budgets equal on all three keep the order I gave them in.

**Several budgets.** Each budget gets its own line and counts independently: if two budgets match the same account
(say `Expenses` and `Expenses:Food`) the same spending is in both lines, and two exactly alike budgets give two
identical lines.

### Examples worth checking

With a ledger holding, in March 2024, 250.00 USD of spending on `Expenses:Food:Groceries`, 90.00 USD on
`Expenses:Food:Dining` and a refund of 10.00 USD on `Expenses:Food:Groceries`, the budget above (400.00 USD a
month from 2024-01-01) over `2024-03` gives `actual` 330.00 USD, `remaining` 70.00 USD, `percent` `82.5`, `over`
False and `accounts` equal to `(("Expenses:Food:Dining", 90.00 USD), ("Expenses:Food:Groceries", 240.00 USD))`. A 300.00 USD budget gives `remaining` -30.00 USD, `percent` `110.0`, `over` True; one exactly used up is not over (`100.0`).

## Recurring transactions

Rent, the phone bill, the yearly insurance, a standing order to the savings account: they happen on a rhythm and
I am tired of typing them in. In `tallybook.recurring` I want to write the rhythm in plain words, attach a
transaction as a template, and get dated copies of it for any stretch of time I ask about. This module only works
out the dates and the copies; storing them (and never making a copy twice) is the storage layer's job.

```python
from datetime import date
from tallybook.recurring import Recurring, parse_schedule, occurrences, expand

rent = Recurring("rent", "monthly on 1", template, start=date(2024, 1, 1))
occurrences(rent, date(2024, 3, 1), date(2024, 5, 31))    # [2024-03-01, 2024-04-01, 2024-05-01]
expand([rent, phone], date(2024, 3, 1), date(2024, 3, 31))  # dated Transactions
```

All dates are `datetime.date`; nothing here looks at the clock.

### The schedule words

`parse_schedule(text)` returns a `Schedule` and understands exactly these shapes:

| text | meaning |
|---|---|
| `daily` | every day |
| `weekly on mon` | every Monday; the day is `mon tue wed thu fri sat sun` |
| `monthly on 5` | the 5th of every month; a number from 1 to 31 |
| `monthly on last` | the last day of every month |
| `yearly on 03-15` | every 15 March; `MM-DD`, two digits each |
| `every 2 weeks from 2024-01-03` | the given date, then every 2 weeks after it |
| `every 3 months from 2024-01-31` | the given date, then every 3 months after it |

The `every` form is `every N UNIT from DATE`: `N` is a whole number of at least 1, `UNIT` is `days`, `weeks`,
`months` or `years` (or the singular `day`, `week`, `month`, `year`, with any `N`), and `DATE` is a real
`YYYY-MM-DD` date.

Capitals and the amount of blank space between the words or around the text do not matter (`Monthly On LAST` is
fine). Anything that is not one of these shapes (`daily on mon`, `weekly`, `monthly on 0`, `monthly on 32`,
`weekly on someday`, `yearly on 13-01`, `yearly on 02-30`, `yearly on 3-15`, `every 0 days from 2024-01-01`,
`every 2 weeks`, `every 2 fortnights from 2024-01-01`, `every 2 weeks from 2024-02-30`, an empty text, a value
that is not text) raises `RecurringError`, a `tallybook.errors.ValidationError` (code `validation`), whose message
names the shapes that are allowed.

A `Schedule` is an immutable, hashable value; schedules that mean the same are equal (`Daily` and `daily`, or
`every 1 week from 2024-01-03` and `every 1 weeks from 2024-01-03`). `str(schedule)` is the canonical text: lower
case, single spaces, `monthly on last`, `yearly on 03-15` with two digits, and in the `every` form the unit
singular when `N` is 1 and plural otherwise (`every 1 week from 2024-01-03`, `every 2 weeks from 2024-01-03`).
Parsing the canonical text gives back an equal schedule.

`schedule.between(start, end)` is the list of the schedule's own dates from `start` to `end`, both included,
ascending (a Schedule knows nothing about a series' start, end or count).

### Which dates a schedule produces

- `daily`: every day. `weekly on mon`: every date that is a Monday.
- `monthly on N`: the Nth day of every month; a month too short for it gets its last day, so `monthly on 31` gives
  31 Jan, 29 Feb 2024, 31 Mar, 30 Apr and `monthly on 30` gives 28 Feb 2023. `monthly on last` is the last day
  whatever the length.
- `yearly on MM-DD`: that day every year; `yearly on 02-29` gives 29 Feb in leap years and 28 Feb in the others.
- `every N days from D` and `every N weeks from D` (a week is 7 days): D, D plus N days (or weeks), plus twice
  that, and so on; nothing before D. `every 10 days from 2024-01-01` gives 1, 11, 21, 31 January, 10 February.
- `every N months from D` and `every N years from D` (a year is 12 months): the k-th date is D moved forward by
  k times N months, counted from D itself and not from the previous date, the day clamped to the end of the month
  when needed; nothing before D. So `every 1 months from 2024-01-31` gives 01-31, 02-29, 03-31, 04-30, 05-31 (no
  drift to the 30th), `every 3 months from 2024-01-31` gives 2024-01-31, 04-30, 07-31, 10-31, 2025-01-31, and
  `every 1 years from 2024-02-29` gives 2024-02-29, then 28 Feb 2025, 2026 and 2027, then 2028-02-29.

### A recurring item

`Recurring(name, schedule, template, start, end=None, count=None)`:

- `name`: text of ASCII letters, digits, `-` and `_`, not beginning with `-` or `_` (`rent`, `phone-bill`, `2024_tax`).
- `schedule`: a `Schedule`, or text, which is parsed with `parse_schedule` (so a bad text raises
  `RecurringError`). The attribute `.schedule` is always a `Schedule`.
- `template`: a `tallybook.model.Transaction`. Its own date means nothing; its payee, narration, flag, tags and
  postings are what the copies are made from.
- `start`: the first day the series may produce a date. `end`: the last day, included, or `None`. `count`: the
  most dates the series ever produces, or `None`; it counts the dates produced from `start` on, so it never
  depends on which stretch of time is asked about later.

The attributes `.name .schedule .template .start .end .count` are readable. Items with equal attributes are equal.
Anything wrong (a name that does not fit, a schedule that is not a `Schedule` or text, a template that is not a
`Transaction`, a `start` that is not a date, an `end` that is not a date or is before `start`, a `count` that is
not an `int` of at least 1, `True` included) is a `RecurringError`.

`occurrences(rec, start, end)` returns the dates of the series within the window `start` to `end`, both
included, ascending, as a list (an `end` before `start` gives `[]`). The series is the schedule's dates that are
on or after `rec.start`, up to and including `rec.end` if there is one, and no more than `rec.count` of them,
counted from the first. Some consequences:

- A start on a day the schedule hits includes that day (`weekly on mon` from Monday 2024-01-01 gives 2024-01-01
  first); `monthly on 5` starting 2024-02-10 gives 2024-03-05 first.
- With `count=3`, a January start and `monthly on 5`, the dates are 5 Jan, 5 Feb, 5 Mar, even when I ask only
  about April to June (nothing comes back then).
- `end` and `count` both apply; whichever stops the series first wins.
- The `every` forms keep the rhythm of the date after `from` even if the item starts later: `every 2 weeks from
  2024-01-03` with `start=2024-01-20` gives 2024-01-31, 2024-02-14, 2024-02-28... (and never anything before
  2024-01-03, even when `start` is earlier).

### Copies of the template

`expand(recs, start, end)` returns a list of new `Transaction` objects, one for every date of every item in the
window, ordered by date, then item name (plain text order), then the item's position in `recs`. A copy has:

- `date` the occurrence date; `payee`, `narration` and `flag` equal to the template's; `id` `None`;
- `postings`: a new list holding the template's postings in order (a posting without an amount stays without one);
- `tags`: a tuple of the template's tags plus the tag `recurring`, each once, sorted.

The template is never changed, and changing a copy's list of postings changes neither the template nor the other
copies. `instantiate(rec, on)` builds the single copy dated `on` the same way (it does not check that `on` is one
of the item's dates).

For example, with a template tagged `home`, `expand([rent], date(2024, 2, 1), date(2024, 3, 31))` for the item
above gives two transactions dated 2024-02-01 and 2024-03-01, each with tags `("home", "recurring")`.

### Two more helpers

`next_occurrence(rec, after)` returns the first date of the series (`start`, `end` and `count` applied as for
`occurrences`) strictly after the date `after`, or `None` when the series has no more dates. For `monthly on 5`
starting 2024-01-01, `after` 2024-02-05 gives 2024-03-05 and `after` 2023-06-01 gives 2024-01-05.

`describe(schedule)` says a schedule in words for a person:

| schedule | text |
|---|---|
| `daily` | `every day` |
| `weekly on mon` | `every Monday` (`Tuesday`, `Wednesday`, `Thursday`, `Friday`, `Saturday`, `Sunday`) |
| `monthly on 5` | `on the 5th of every month` |
| `monthly on last` | `on the last day of every month` |
| `yearly on 03-15` | `every year on 15 March` |
| `every 2 weeks from 2024-01-03` | `every 2 weeks from 2024-01-03` |
| `every 1 month from 2024-01-31` | `every month from 2024-01-31` |

A day of the month is an English ordinal (1st, 2nd, 3rd, 4th, 11th, 12th, 13th, 21st, 22nd, 23rd, 31st); a day in
`yearly on` is a plain number (`every year on 5 July`). In the `every` form a step of 1 drops the number and uses
the singular unit (`every day from DATE`, `every week`, `every month`, `every year`); other steps keep the number
and the plural unit (`every 3 months from ...`).

## Reports

This is what I really want the tool for: look at the book and tell me where I stand. In `tallybook.reports` I
want six reports, each a plain Python `dict` I can `json.dumps` straight away, a function that draws any of them as
text, and one that turns them into CSV.

```python
from tallybook.reports import (trial_balance, balance_sheet, income_statement, cashflow, register, net_worth,
                               render_text, report_to_csv, ReportError)

report = income_statement(ledger, Period.parse("2024-03"))
print(render_text(report), end="")
```

Every report function takes a `tallybook.ledger.Ledger` first and does not change it. `ReportError` is a
`tallybook.errors.ValidationError` (code `validation`).

### Conventions all reports share

- A report `dict` contains only dicts, lists, strings, booleans, `None` and integers. Its key `"report"` is
  `"trial_balance"`, `"balance_sheet"`, `"income_statement"`, `"cashflow"`, `"register"` or `"net_worth"`.
- Money is always `{"amount": "12.50", "currency": "USD"}` (amount text with the currency's own number of
  decimals, a leading `-` when negative, no thousands separators). Dates are `"YYYY-MM-DD"` text.
- The type of an account comes from its first path segment: `Assets` asset, `Liabilities` liability, `Equity`
  equity, `Income` income, `Expenses` expense.
- Lists of accounts are sorted by account path as plain text, character by character (`Expenses:Food-X` comes
  before `Expenses:Food:Alpha` because `-` sorts before `:`), then by currency code; lists of money per currency by
  currency code. Postings are never rolled up into parent accounts unless stated.
- A zero balance is left out of an account list. (Lists of money per currency are described report by report.)
- Dates mean whole days, both ends of a `Period` included. A "balance on D" counts every posting dated on or
  before D.
- Percentages are text with exactly one decimal (`"5.7"`, `"100.0"`, `"-2.5"`), rounded to the nearest tenth of a
  percent, an exact half going away from zero (0.25 becomes `0.3`); a zero result is `"0.0"`, never `"-0.0"`.
- Converting to one currency (`convert_to="EUR"`) uses the exchange rates the ledger knows: its attribute `rates`,
  the `RateTable` it was created with (an empty table if none), at the rate in force on the date given below, one
  amount at a time, as the currency module converts money. A missing rate raises the currency module's own
  `CurrencyError` as it is, and so does a `convert_to` that is not a known currency.

### The sample book used below

Accounts `Assets:Bank:Checking`, `Assets:Cash`, `Liabilities:Card`, `Equity:Opening`, `Income:Salary`,
`Expenses:Food`, `Expenses:Rent`; all USD. The transactions, with ids 1 to 8 in this order:

| id | date | payee | postings |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 2024-01-01 | Opening | Checking +1000.00, Equity:Opening -1000.00 |
| 2 | 2024-03-01 | Acme | Checking +2500.00, Income:Salary -2500.00 |
| 3 | 2024-03-02 | Market | Expenses:Food +42.50, Checking -42.50 |
| 4 | 2024-03-05 | Landlord | Expenses:Rent +900.00, Liabilities:Card -900.00 |
| 5 | 2024-03-10 | ATM | Assets:Cash +100.00, Checking -100.00 |
